extracted.intended_audience: advertising and marketing researchers; advertising practitioners and survey/measurement specialists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and findings for designing, measuring, and interpreting advertising and consumer information-seeking research (survey design, multivariate analysis, physiological measurement, Q-methodology) and implications for advertising practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AID and MCA for interaction analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sophisticated computer techniques--AID (Automatic Interaction Detector) and MCA (Multiple Classification Analysis)--were used in tandem to estimate the separate and combined effects of factors and determine which variables, in combination, best distinguish individuals with different levels of information-seeking behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the combination of AID and MCA as an empirical method to (1) determine interacting component variables that form useful complex predictors, (2) investigate interrelationships between explanatory variables and behavior, and (3) determine overall predictive power. Use these techniques when single-variable analyses fail to explain observed differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for combined effects / interactions of explanatory variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When considered singly, personal and product variables often do not adequately explain observed differences in behavior; separate variables interact with one another in affecting behavior, making combined influence crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate complex explanatory variables (e.g., 'life style') from groups of interacting component variables. Empirically identify which component variables interact and consider using the combined construct as a new predictor to improve prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust advertising timing and content to purchase decision duration
rubrics_metrics.description: About half the buyers of major consumer durables spend only a few weeks making the purchase decision, indicating a rapid turnover of prospective purchasers actively seeking information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising strategists should adjust the timing and content of advertising to account for rapid turnover (concentrate reach during decision windows; tailor message urgency and information density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment by previous experience and satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of information-seeking behavior varies as a function of previous experience and level of satisfaction with the product category; learning can reduce subsequent information-seeking and decision time but not all selectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by prior experience and satisfaction; expect reduced search and decision time among experienced/satisfied consumers but persistent selectivity in choice (e.g., single-brand consideration among inexperienced buyers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize prior advertising exposure (pre-market awareness) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people regularly observe advertising prior to their awareness of being in the market; this prior effect can substantially limit their subsequent information search once they are aware of being in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting information-search behavior, control for or measure prior exposure to advertising — it can bias or reduce active search and should inform media planning and message sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumers use multiple information sources; media play complementary roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers use more than one type of information source before buying a consumer durable; advertising was seldom the only source used, and different media were found to serve different and complementary roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single medium dominates; design multi-source/media strategies that leverage complementary roles (e.g., awareness vs. evaluation). Avoid claiming media monopoly in decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey question type critically affects source-ranking (aided vs unaided)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because both aided and unaided recall questions were asked regarding ranking of information sources, it was possible to compare methods; advertising frequently ranks low with unaided recall questions, but other question types show advertising is widely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully choose and compare question types and ranking criteria before accepting consumer judgments of information source influence. Use multiple question formats (aided, unaided, prompted ranking) and cross-validate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q-Methodology: card-sorting procedure and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Q-Methodology requires individuals to sort objects (often cards with statements) into evaluative categories along an eleven-point scale with instructions to distribute judgments in a 'quasi-normal' manner and specify exact numbers per category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement Q-technique by: using an 11-point (or specified) scale, enforcing a quasi-normal distribution (prescribed counts per category), instructing respondents clearly, and then grouping similar response patterns via factor-analytic procedures. Use Q to segment on subjective values (not to estimate relative group size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factor analysis to group subjective response patterns (Q results)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Q-sorting procedure is carried out, individuals can be grouped by the similarity of their responses, determined by factor-analytic statistical procedures to identify what 'groups' exist for a product/service/message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus Q-analysis on discovering subjective-value segments and interpretations of valuing; avoid misusing Q to estimate population proportions. Ensure factor-analytic methods and rotation choices are appropriate to the Q-sample size and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design field studies with diverse samples and locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Field studies were conducted in different cities (Cleveland, Philadelphia, Lansing) and included diverse respondents (black and white adults; children in various environments) to study communication behaviors of the urban poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching segmented populations (e.g., urban poor), include multiple locations and demographic groups to capture variation in media use, attitudes, and motivations. Use mixed samples (age, race, urban/suburban/rural) as appropriate to research questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret television and newspaper exposure as predictors of information awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-income families were exposed to more hours of television and use of newspapers related to awareness of expert/professional information sources; interpersonal traits (gregariousness) also related to awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure multiple media exposures and interpersonal contact diversity when modeling awareness of expert sources. Consider TV hours and newspaper use as predictors in models of information access and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literature review plus survey to select lab experimental measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The research combined an extensive literature review and a mail survey of 668 respondents to determine which physiological equipment to test in the laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before lab testing, conduct systematic literature reviews and practitioner surveys to identify commonly used measures and problems; let findings inform which physiological or other measures warrant experimental validity/reliability testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate physiological measures for sensitivity, validity, and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus was to determine how much is known about the sensitivity, validity, and reliability of various types of physiological equipment; laboratory experiments tested selected measures (GSR, PDR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess physiological measures (e.g., galvanic skin response, pupil dilation) through both survey and lab validation work. Prioritize measures with demonstrated sensitivity and establish clear validity and reliability evidence for the targeted marketing problem (e.g., visual perception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware ambiguous stimulus attribution in physiological measures
rubrics_metrics.description: While most physiological measures appear sensitive to changes in stimulus strength, it is not always easy to identify unambiguously the stimulus that is causing the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design physiological experiments with tight stimulus controls, counterbalancing, and complementary measures to reduce ambiguity about causation. Interpret physiological changes cautiously and triangulate with behavioral/self-report data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand managerial use of new product information (test marketing vs cheaper data)
rubrics_metrics.description: More expensive information from test marketing is generally not used to make 'go' or 'no-go' decisions, but rather to confirm or refine decisions already made on the basis of less costly data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing new product research, recognize how managers will use data: inexpensive predictive indicators may drive decisions, while expensive studies serve refinement/confirmation. Align research scope and cost with managerial decision needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select 'predictors' rather than heavy users for concept testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers identified as 'predictors' (based on past predictive accuracy) predicted new product success twice as accurately as 'heavy users' or 'new-product triers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recruiting respondents for product-concept testing, consider using panels of proven 'predictors' (identified by track record) rather than defaulting to heavy users/triers. Investigate demographic and personality correlates to identify predictors in a target market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment markets by promotion-effectiveness (advertising vs sampling)
rubrics_metrics.description: For some individuals advertising is the most effective promotion; for others, new product sampling is most effective, suggesting potential market segmentation by promotion-effectiveness criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate heterogeneity in promotional responsiveness; design experiments or tests to classify subgroups by which promotion (ad, sampling, etc.) elicits adoption, and tailor promotion mix accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience prejudice effects when using integrated advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: An experimental investigation of racial prejudice and integrated advertising indicated that more highly prejudiced whites react adversely to advertisements featuring non-whites; less prejudiced whites respond similarly to integrated and white-only ads; responses tend to carry over to products and companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning integrated advertising, assess target-audience prejudice levels and weigh potential adverse reactions against benefits. Test creative and measure carryover effects to brand/company evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design message strategy with self-concept findings in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's actual or 'real' self-concept was more predictive of brand preference for both conspicuous and inconspicuous products than was his aspired or 'ideal' self-concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In message design, emphasize appeals that align with the target's actual self-concept rather than assumed ideal-self appeals; segment messages where self-attitude effects are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use industrial/institutional advertising strategically for organizational buyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising can be particularly helpful to little-known suppliers in industrial markets; particular types of institutional advertisements are more effective in this role than product advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For B2B/industrial contexts, consider institutional advertising to build supplier awareness and credibility, especially for lesser-known firms; test ad types with organizational buyers to identify most effective formats.
